passage: Note from Zainab, English teacher, about Pema, Class 10. Pema handed in an essay on the school library that opened: "The multifaceted utilisation of the institutional literary repository is undeniably of paramount significance." Read aloud, it took Pema four attempts to say what the sentence meant: "The library is useful." Pema said quietly, "I thought simple words would sound childish." I asked Pema to underline the three main points and rewrite each in the plainest sentence possible. The second draft came out at half the length. Pema read it aloud and said it sounded a bit plain but was easy to follow. Next step: plain first, then one strong word only where it earns its place. - Zainab

qa.q: What did Pema say the long opening sentence meant?
qa.a: Pema said it meant that the library is useful.

qa.q: What was Pema worried about when choosing long words?
qa.a: Pema worried that simple words would sound childish, and wanted to seem clever.

qa.q: What did Zainab ask Pema to do to fix the essay?
qa.a: Zainab asked Pema to underline the three main points and rewrite each in the plainest sentence possible.

qa.q: How did Zainab see the second draft compared with the first?
qa.a: As clearer and half the length, and a better base for adding one strong word where it is needed.

grounding: Shows a teenager stretching sentences with long words to seem clever and a teacher's plain-language fix.

passage: Friday. Got my history essay back from Uma Ma'am, covered in red circles. I had written things like "the aforementioned emperor's magnificent administrative endeavours" because I wanted to sound like a professor. Ma'am wrote beside it: "What did the emperor actually do?" I stared at that for ages. He built roads and set up a tax system. That's the whole sentence! On Saturday I tried it on the next paragraph: "The emperor's officers measured land and collected tax at fixed rates." My cousin Dev read both and said the second was clearer, which I hate. It feels smaller, but Dev understood it straight away. - Arohi

qa.q: What did Uma Ma'am write beside the fancy sentence?
qa.a: Ma'am wrote: "What did the emperor actually do?"

qa.q: What did Arohi feel when Dev said the plain sentence was clearer?
qa.a: Reluctant and a bit annoyed, because the plain version feels smaller even though it is clearer.

qa.q: What step helped Arohi turn the sentence into something clear?
qa.a: Asking what the emperor actually did and writing that plainly: officers measured land and collected tax at fixed rates.

qa.q: Why did Dev understand the second version straight away?
qa.a: It used plain words and said one clear thing, so Dev did not have to decode it.

grounding: Shows a teenager padding an essay with long words to sound impressive and learning that plain writing serves the reader better.

passage:
In Lagos, Nkechi spent Sunday evening on her history essay. She wanted Mr Adeyemi to think she was brilliant. So she wrote: "The multifaceted ramifications of colonial infrastructural paradigms necessitate a comprehensive reevaluation of contemporaneous socioeconomic trajectories." She read it three times and felt proud.
Her friend Omar read it on the bus next morning. "Nkechi, what does this mean?"
She opened her mouth. "It means… the railways were built to take things out, not to help people move around. And that still affects things now."
"Then why didn't you write that?"
She shrugged. "It sounds too simple."
On Friday, the essay came back. Beside her favourite sentence Mr Adeyemi had written: "I read this four times. What are you trying to say?" Under the conclusion, which she had written in a hurry and plainly, he had written: "This is clear and strong. More of this."

qa.q: What did Mr Adeyemi write beside Nkechi's favourite sentence?
qa.a: "I read this four times. What are you trying to say?"

qa.q: Why did Nkechi feel proud of her long sentence at first?
qa.a: Nkechi wanted to seem brilliant, and the long words made the sentence feel impressive to her.

qa.q: What could Nkechi try in her next essay?
qa.a: Nkechi could write each point the way she explained it to Omar, in plain words, and save long words for when they are really needed.

qa.q: How does Omar see Nkechi's sentence?
qa.a: Omar finds it confusing, and he points out that her plain spoken explanation was much clearer.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who writes long words to sound clever, confusing the reader, while her plain explanation is far clearer.

passage:
In the school newsletter room, Tenzin handed his article about the new water coolers to the student editor, Elizabeth.
She read the first paragraph aloud. "In light of the aforementioned considerations pertaining to hydration infrastructure, it is incumbent upon the student body to…" She stopped. "Tenzin. What do you want them to do?"
"Use the coolers instead of buying bottles."
"Then say that."
He frowned. "It'll sound like a Class Six kid wrote it."
Elizabeth pulled out last month's issue and pointed to the most-read piece: short sentences, no big words. "Kids read this one. Yours they'll skip after one line."
Tenzin sat at the corner desk and rewrote it: "We have four new water coolers. Use them. Every bottle you don't buy is one less in the bin." It felt flat to him. But on Monday, two Class Eight boys stopped him in the corridor to say they'd started refilling.

qa.q: How many new water coolers does Tenzin's rewrite mention?
qa.a: It mentions four new water coolers.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the rewritten version?
qa.a: Tenzin felt it was flat and a bit childish, worried it would sound like a Class Six kid wrote it.

qa.q: Which version worked better, and why?
qa.a: The short, plain version worked better, because readers could see the request at once and two boys actually started refilling.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Tenzin's first draft?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees it as hard to follow and likely to be skipped, so she asks what he actually wants readers to do.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose long, stretched sentences make an article hard to follow, and whose plain rewrite works better for readers.

passage:
Dear Madhav bhaiya,
You asked how my college essay was going. Badly, then better.
My first draft had sentences like, "My indefatigable passion for the multidimensional realm of biological sciences has been cultivated through a plethora of experiential engagements." I thought it sounded like a topper. I was very proud of the word "plethora."
Our English teacher read it and asked me one question: "What actually happened?" So I told her. When I was in Class Nine, Nani's goat got sick and I sat with the village vet for a whole afternoon, handing him things and asking a hundred questions. That's when I started liking biology.
She said, "Write that." It felt too small, almost embarrassing. But when I read the new version to Amma, she went quiet and then said, "That's you."
I'm attaching both. Please tell me honestly which one you'd want to read.
Your sister,
Vidya

qa.q: What word was Vidya very proud of?
qa.a: Vidya was very proud of the word "plethora."

qa.q: How did Vidya feel about the plain version at first?
qa.a: Vidya felt it was too small, almost embarrassing, compared with the grand words of the first draft.

qa.q: What question from the teacher could help any writer who is padding?
qa.a: "What actually happened?" because it pulls the writer back to the real story instead of impressive words.

qa.q: How did Amma react to the new version?
qa.a: Amma went quiet and then said, "That's you," showing she was moved and recognised her daughter in it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who pads an essay with long words to sound impressive and learns that a plain, true story is better for the reader.

passage: "Kashish, you asked what I learned at the science fair. I'm Nilesh, and I learned I was showing off. My project was simple: which cloth keeps water in a clay pot coolest. But on the poster I wrote, 'This investigation endeavours to elucidate the thermodynamic efficacy of diverse textile coverings upon earthenware vessels.' I thought it sounded like a real scientist. The judge read it twice and asked, 'So... what did you do?' Then a Class Four kid stood in front of my poster for a whole minute, frowning, and walked off to the volcano next door. That hurt more than the judge. So that evening I rewrote the top line: 'Which cloth keeps water in a clay pot coolest? We tested five.' It felt almost too plain, like I'd become less clever. But the next morning three little kids stayed, and one of them asked me a proper question."

qa.q: What was Nilesh's project really testing?
qa.a: Which cloth keeps water in a clay pot coolest.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when the Class Four kid walked off to the volcano?
qa.a: Nilesh felt hurt and embarrassed, more than by the judge, because the poster had lost the very people it was for.

qa.q: Which version of the poster worked better, and why?
qa.a: The plain question with "We tested five", because readers understood it at once, so children stayed and asked real questions.

qa.q: How might the judge have experienced the first poster?
qa.a: The judge was probably confused, reading it twice and still needing to ask what Nilesh had actually done.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose long, impressive-sounding words make a science-fair poster hard to follow, and who finds plain writing works better for readers.
